title: Hitting a wall developing the game
author: Significant-Neck-520
selftext:
Claude Opus 5.5 has been delivering so much content so fast that the early development of the RPG I'm making has been a blast. I was so happy with the generated art that I posted it on itch.io (not going to spam the link today though). It actually has many issues but it is consistent, I kind of liked the result.

Now I'm at the stage where some things aren't where I want them, and fixing them is a token black hole: iterating over and over for little gains.

In particular, I have a dissolve effect on geometry that's in front of the characters and blocking the view, and I can't get it working without lots of artifacts. It also exposes all the underlying issues with the generated geometry, like double faces and z-fighting. No screenshots, sorry, I'm on mobile.

This is part of the process, though. The parts AI isn't getting right are where we have to figure things out to keep the project moving. I guess that's the difference between a prototype and a finished product. Prototyping is so much more fun, and I miss that phase. I have a bunch of new monsters I want Claude to model, but the game needs the z-fighting fixed, not new monsters.

To be fair, this stage used to be much worse without AI. You could spend months trying to get one thing working right. Now it's days of iteration, but it still feels like a lot of work with little to show for it.

Right now I'm fighting the urge to start another project on the side. How do you all get through these phases? Do you push through, or let yourself prototype something fun to keep the motivation going?

replies.author: cckynv
replies.body:
Two of my main rules for the AI when we're building systems:

1. Build Reusable Systems: Make modular, reusable frameworks. Encapsulate common patterns and decisions logic into reusable components.

2. Tuning-First Design: Any value that affects game feel is built as a serialized field. Do not rely on hardcoded values.

comments.author: JWalter89
comments.body:
I find that AI will tend to iterate on what's already there when actually that system might just need an entirely different approach.

Focus on a problem, and then ask Claude to look at removing that system, and starting again now that the requirements have shifted.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Yep, you absolutely*,* absolutely need to question its design choices sometimes.  I had Claude pushing me towards something totally wild last night until I stopped it and straight up went "this seems completely over-engineered for a simple problem.  Maybe we do this, but first we need to evaluate it against what we're actually attempting to accomplish and do some research on how other games in this space handle it."

Ended up trimming it down to about a fourth of the work it would have been for a solution that's a lot closer to the target, though the original still might get implemented sparingly for visual polish waaaaay later.

If you don't approach working with AI like you're a Designer and just let it churn out whatever random nonsense it thinks is what you asked for, you're gonna end up like OP - hip deep in a soup of buggy nonsense that's not shippable that you have no idea how to fix.

comments.author: LeTrifluvien
comments.body:
An another idea is to ask for a detailed specification of the effect you have now without technical details, the you ask in a new conversation, outside of the context of your app, five mockup of the effects. Then you modify your favorite mockup and then you go back into you app context to replace the previous effect with the mockup one.

Taking the conversation outside of the context of your game will allow the AI to have a fresh view on the solution.

replies.author: LeTrifluvien
replies.body:
Something worth doing at that point is to restart your project from scratch, not even kidding. 

Now that you know exactly what you want, you take a few days to properly create the specifications, and build one piece at the time from the foundations. 

This will make your code much more clean as you probably have a very Frankenstein code base since you changed direction multiple times and it will get harder and harder to make changes.

Don't build monsters.

comments.author: zoopesh
comments.body: Push through it. The best thing to do is to tell it what you need done and ask it what YOU can do to make it happen instead of fully relying on it. The AI will tell you what you can do, asking you to provide stuff to it or do certain steps before handing it the remaining portion. The thing about opus 5.5 is that it knows what it's not good at or cannot do and it helps you work around that by suggesting what you can do. Expecting it to do everything in a project from 0-100 will never have you finishing a game. You will just be stuck making prototypes forever

comments.author: Cassp3
comments.body:
I feel like anyone whos actually making or made something very quickly learns that the AI is simultaneously smart and dumb as all hell at the same time. 

You can tell it to make a feature, and it will make an extremely unoptimized piece of junk that does actually work. And the optimization for it is extremely simple. So you wonder, why the hell did it implement this piece of shit, like obviously I didn't want this script running every single frame.

That's because the AI needs serious handholding. Over time you learn the things that it will mess up so you make sure to double check it, make sure it did it right.

I've found, you have to figure out the core frameworks of your game very early, and build that first. Not the art itself, but things like world streaming, z layering, pathing, as you said how the game renders walls that obscure the camera.

These are things that it's best to mess around with very early, so you're not hundreds of hours in and realise, wait my pathing is a mess.

Vibe coding is a skill in itself, like most things, you get better over time.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
I actually found a side project to be incredibly useful here for maintaining momentum through long debugging periods. If your main project is far enough along you could also find other 'fun' tasks to do that are requirements you'd need to handle anyway, that maybe would give you motivation. For instance while slamming your head on the debugging wall, you could start looking into SFX and music and planning out your soundscape or mocking up UIs that aren't finalized or creating/tweaking assets, or playtesting what you already have. All of these things, in my experience, can continue to keep the motivation flowing and avoid distraction. But even a side project is not harmful. You're likely to learn things you didn't know, assuming it's different. You might be able to incorporate aspects into your main project. Or maybe you end up having so much more fun with it, (just have to be careful not to fall into the trap of 'newness') that it ends up becoming your main. I've ended up taking mechanics from one side project and the overall style from another and merging them into my main project. I also established a better workflow in one of those which I ended up moving over as well and it saved me a tremendous amount of tokens long term.

I'd definitely avoid setting aside the main project though while you do these things. Keep the debugs running, always take the time first to address the issues present, and when AI is chugging along, use that time to explore other things.

Though personally I find one of the best ways to clear these hurdles is to do a bunch of your own research on the issue and see if you can find things to point the AI in the right direction. Can't count the number of times I've found old reddit or stack overflow posts which the AI didn't ever find in its own research, which happened to have the solution (or at least providing the threads was enough to get the AI to figure out what was going on within one more iteration.)

comments.author: RedTowerDev
comments.body:
We definitely went through this phase too, where the fun stops and the work starts. AI doesn’t really change that part of game development. Prototyping has always been fun, but polishing and fixing things that aren’t working is still a grind.  
AI has made our current RPG a lot larger in scope than anything we’ve been able to do before, and we’re very happy with that. But we’ve also had several points where the whole project nearly went off the rails. The daily grind really isn’t that different, even if we’re getting a lot more done.  
I’ve found I’m more productive if I keep a few tasks around that I actually enjoy. Today I should be fixing some ugly hair colors on our female sprites and updating our Steam screenshots. Instead, I have one potential screenshot replacement showing off our new NPC roleplay systems, which are potentially getting put in the game way ahead of schedule.  
A few days ago I also spent time building a pretty cool dragon ruler for one of our factions, well ahead of when we actually needed him. But that stuff still adds value to the game, and sometimes doing something fun is what keeps you working through the boring parts.  
It is as important as ever to keep getting the less fun stuff done though!

comments.author: Radiant_Mind33
comments.body:
Every A.I dev will hit that same wall.

You cant just keep prompting at light speed and expect a completed game/project.

Gemini and I built a whole game engine snippet by snippet. Then we tore it all down and built it again snippet by snippet. Plus, the whole time I was testing every little thing for hours.

IOW, when we need to fix the code or any geometry, we know exactly where to go. It doesn't matter if it's Codex, or Muse, or Claude either. There's no token black hole. How could there be? The canvas render is on like 25k of x file. I suppose JavaScript is just way easier, so there's that.  But still, if you don't know the code at all and don't know what to tell the LLM, it's a serious problem.

comments.author: Witty_Visual7750

Finishing a game is a different challenge from starting one, and these frustrating phases are part of the process.

comments.author: CheeseNuke
comments.body:
Start from first principles. This is where learning proper software engineering is useful: restate your problem, gather all the context, identify your constraints, then map out your solution accordingly. Ask for visualizations - I like [diagram-design](https://github.com/cathrynlavery/diagram-design). Don't implement anything until you have a firm understanding of the system design and all your functional boundaries.

IMO, your life will be easier if you focus on a modular approach and enforce constraints via compilation / structural guards. In other words, make a particular failure mode impossible _by construction_. Think shared API contracts, libraries/functionality, etc.
